newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Brazzaville lull, confusion over ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville lull, confusion over ceasefire.

text.p: Shooting subsided in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Monday after now ritual dawn salvoes and sources close to mediators said they expected the warring parties to start observing a ceasefire.

President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, initialled a ceasefire agreement on Saturday to halt over a month of bloody political and ethnic clashes but there was confusion over the timing.
"For an hour the guns have gone silent under instructions," one source close to the mediators said in Brazzaville on Monday morning.

A mediation committee under Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas was meeting on Monday. "I understand that the military commanders are going to attempt to find ways of applying the ceasefire today," one source said.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who helped negotiate the truce proposed by Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, said on Sunday it would start formally at midnight (2300 GMT) on Monday.
Lissouba's spokesman Gregoire Lefouba had said the truce would begin at midnight on Sunday but witnesses reported heavy overnight exchanges between the two sides.

Sahnoun told BBC radio on Sunday that talks would take place in Gabon's capital Libreville by Tuesday or Wednesday on national reconciliation and creating an environment for elections some time over the next two months.

The bloody showdown in the capital of the oil-producing former French colony began on June 5 when soldiers surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of a now-postponed July 27 presidential election.
The clashes and indiscriminate shellfire have killed hundreds of people, many of them civilians, medical workers say.
Diplomatic sources say the only real hope of a lasting truce is to persuade heavily-armed rival soldiers and militiamen on barricades across Brazzaville to leave the streets.
With plans for a U.N.-sponsored, mainly African peacekeeping force taking shape, Sahnoun said the militia issue would be dealt with in the talks.
He said the warring parties and neighbouring countries wanted a peace force deployed, adding: "It will be an important psychological factor to enhance the peace process."
Lissouba's mandate expires at the end of August. He says the constitution allows a 90-day extension to organise elections. Sassou demands a national salvation government.
Lissouba, Sassou and Kolelas, whose militia has kept out of the latest fighting, planned to contest the July 27 election.
Kolelas's militia was at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election.
